slides.text: You can already append, copy, remove and insert. Now you will use a slice as a stack and as a queue, then filter in place, clone, build rows and shift values with `copy`.

A stack takes values at the end and gives them back from the end. A queue takes values at the end and gives them back from the front.

A slice is both, with `append` and a cut. No extra type is needed.
Taking a value out is a cut, not a delete: the slice gets shorter, and the next `append` writes over the value that was cut off.

exercises.title: A stack
exercises.guide: Push values to a slice and pop them.

chunks.guide: A stack takes values at the end. Pushing is an `append`.
chunks.text:
var stack []string
    stack = append(stack, "a")
    stack = append(stack, "b")
    stack = append(stack, "c")
    fmt.Println(stack)

chunks.guide: Popping reads the last value, then cuts it off.
chunks.text:
top := stack[len(stack)-1]
    stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]
    fmt.Println(top, stack)

chunks.guide: The next push takes the place of the popped value.

output.text:
[a b c]
c [a b]
[a b d] 3

exercises.title: Push and pop functions
exercises.guide: Wrap the stack operations in two functions.

chunks.guide: Push returns the longer stack.
Pop returns two things: the shorter stack and the value taken.
Both results are stored. Popping the last value leaves an empty slice.
chunks.text:
func main() {
    var s []int
    s = push(s, 1)
    s = push(s, 2)
    s, v := pop(s)
    fmt.Println(v, s)
    s, v = pop(s)
    fmt.Println(v, s, len(s))
}

exercises.title: Push and peek
exercises.guide: Push a value onto the stack, then read its top value.

exercises.title: A queue
exercises.guide: Add values at the end and take them from the front.

chunks.guide: A queue takes values at the end, like a stack.
It gives values from the front: read index 0, then cut it off.
chunks.text:
first := queue[0]
    queue = queue[1:]
    fmt.Println(first, queue)

chunks.guide: Values keep joining at the end while others leave from the front.

output.text:
[a b c]
a [b c]
[b c d] 3

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Cutting the end leaves [1 2], the append makes it [1 2 4], and cutting the front leaves [2 4], which has 2 values.

slides.text:
Sometimes you want a fresh slice, not a window on the old values. Appending to `nil` builds one, and `copy` fills one you made yourself.

Other times you want to reuse the old values on purpose: filtering into the same storage, or shifting values inside one slice.

exercises.title: Filter in place
exercises.guide: Keep some values without making a new slice.

chunks.guide: Start from an empty piece of the same slice.
Each kept value is appended into the space the loop already passed.
No new storage was needed, but the original was written over on the way. Why the storage is shared comes in the Slice capacity module.

exercises.title: Clone with append
exercises.guide: Make a separate copy in one line.

chunks.guide: Appending to a `nil` slice builds a new one with the same values.

notes.text: A nil slice of ints to append onto.

chunks.guide: It is a real copy: the two slices do not share values.
Cloning nothing gives nothing: the result is still `nil`.
chunks.text:
var none []int
    c := append([]int(nil), none...)
    fmt.Println(c == nil, len(c))

exercises.title: Build rows
exercises.guide: Build a grid by appending rows.

chunks.guide: A slice of rows, empty for now.
Build each row with `append`, then append the row to the grid.
A grid of three rows of three values.

exercises.title: Shift values left
exercises.guide: Move the values of a slice one place left.

chunks.guide: `copy` works inside one slice. The parts overlap, and each value moves one place left.
`copy` returns how many values moved. The last value is a leftover.
Cut off the leftover.

exercises.title: Shift and trim
exercises.guide: Shift the values one place left, then keep only the values that moved.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `b` starts as a separate copy of `a`, then grows to [1 2 1 2]. Setting `b[0]` changes only `b`, and `a` stays [1 2].
